title: Learn by Doing: Exceptions and File Input and Output
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on exceptions and files, each with its model answer, and the method taught from nothing.
intro: Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only, and a whole question of the 24/25 paper is files, end to end: define the classes, debug a snippet, state what the file contains, then write a program that creates it, writes records and reads them back.

lockin.big: "Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws, and the compiler enforces it. Unchecked ones are your bugs, and it does not."
lockin.sub: FileWriter with true appends, without it overwrites. try-with-resources closes the file for you, whatever happens.

methodFrames.teach:
An exception is an error raised while the program runs. Java splits them in two, and the difference is who is responsible.

public class Kinds {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {1, 2, 3};        try {            System.out.println(a[5]);        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {            System.out.println("unchecked: " + e.getMessage());        }        try {            System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("ten"));        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {            System.out.println("unchecked: " + e.getMessage());        } finally {            System.out.println("finally always runs");        }    }}
Outputunchecked: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3
unchecked: For input string: "ten"
finally always runs
methodFrames.ask: Which kind does the compiler force you to handle, and what is the other kind usually caused by?

methodFrames.check: Checked ones. Unchecked ones come from bugs in the code.
methodFrames.teach:
Checked exceptions are the ones the compiler forces you to catch or declare, IOException and FileNotFoundException among them, and they are about the world outside the program. Unchecked ones extend RuntimeException, are your own bugs, and the compiler says nothing: the two above are unchecked.

Three differences for the 25/26 question: checked are checked at compile time, unchecked at run time; checked must be handled or declared, unchecked need not be; checked signal outside failures, unchecked signal programming faults.
methodFrames.ask: In that listing, when did finally run, and when would it not?

methodFrames.teach:
It ran after the catch, and it runs whether or not an exception was thrown, which is why it is where files and connections are closed. It is skipped only if the JVM itself exits.

throw raises an exception now; throws in a header declares that this method may raise one and will not handle it. One letter apart, and the exam asks for both.

import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.IOException;public class Records {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (FileWriter out = new FileWriter("students.txt")) {            out.write("20/1234,Ada,4.6\n");            out.write("20/1235,Grace,3.9\n");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("could not write: " + e.getMessage());        }        try (FileWriter more = new FileWriter("students.txt", true)) {            more.write("20/1236,Chinwe,4.1\n");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("could not append: " + e.getMessage());        }        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("students.txt"))) {            String line;            int n = 0;            while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {                n++;                String[] parts = line.split(",");                System.out.println(n + ". " + parts[1] + " has " + parts[2]);            }            System.out.println(n + " records");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("could not read: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}
Output1. Ada has 4.6
2. Grace has 3.9
3. Chinwe has 4.1
3 records
methodFrames.ask: Now files. Which class writes, which reads, and what does the second argument true do?

methodFrames.check: FileWriter writes, BufferedReader with FileReader reads, and true appends.
methodFrames.teach:
FileWriter writes, BufferedReader wrapped around a FileReader reads a line at a time, and the second argument true means APPEND. Without it the file is emptied the moment it is opened, which is the difference between adding a record and destroying every record.

Note the loop: while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) is the shape to memorise, because readLine returns null at the end of the file.
methodFrames.ask: Every open above sits inside try (...) rather than before it. What is that called, and what does it save you?

methodFrames.check: try-with-resources: it closes the file for you.
methodFrames.teach:
try-with-resources, which 24/25 asks you to define. Anything opened in those brackets is closed automatically when the block ends, whether it ended normally or by an exception, so no finally block and no forgotten close.

PrintWriter is the other writer to know: it wraps a file and gives you println and printf, so it writes formatted lines the way System.out does.
methodFrames.ask: Last, the one that costs marks in a debug question: what must a method that opens a file either do or declare?

methodFrames.check: Catch IOException or declare throws IOException.
methodFrames.teach: Either catch IOException, or declare throws IOException in its header. IOException is checked, so leaving it out is a compile error and is a favourite planted fault. Check the imports too: java.io.* or the four classes by name.

exam.answer:
Q1 b · three differences: checked vs unchecked · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. When they are detected. Checked exceptions are checked by the compiler at compile time; unchecked exceptions occur at run time and the compiler does not examine them.
  2. Whether you must handle them. A checked exception must be either caught in a try-catch or declared with throws, or the code will not compile. An unchecked exception carries no such obligation.
  3. What causes them. Checked exceptions represent conditions outside the program's control (a missing file, a failed network call), whereas unchecked exceptions represent programming errors (dereferencing null, a bad index, dividing by zero).

Examples (add them; they cost one line and prove the point): checked: IOException, FileNotFoundException, ClassNotFoundException. Unchecked: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException.

Where the marks are: three distinct axes. Writing "one is checked and one is not" three different ways scores one mark. See Unit 10.1.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, The file question, 13 marks

scenario.text:
(13 marks)B. A college admin office needs a program to record and review student details (ID, name, CGPA) using basic file I/O. Using only java.io.FileWriter, java.io.FileReader, java.io.BufferedReader, java.io.BufferedWriter, and java.io.IOException (or its subclasses), write a complete program that does the following:

i.    Create a file named input.txt and write the details (student ID, name, CGPA) of at least three students into it using FileWriter, one student per line. Wrap the writing logic in a try-catch block that handles any exception that may occur.

ii.   Read student details from a file named output.txt using FileReader and print each line to the console exactly as it appears in the file. Handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a file name, opens the file, counts the number of lines (student records) it contains, and returns that count. This method must handle its own exceptions internally.

iv.  Ensure every file resource opened is properly closed (either in a finally block or via try-with-resources) and that every catch block prints a clear, specific message describing what went wrong.

Console output (System.out) is acceptable throughout.

exam.answer:
Q3 b · student records with basic file i/o · 13 MARKS
  1. creates input.txt and writes at least three students (ID, name, CGPA) into it with FileWriter, one per line, wrapped in try-catch;
  2. reads student details from output.txt with FileReader and prints each line exactly as it appears, handling any exception including the case where output.txt does not exist;
  3. has a method that takes a file name, counts the lines, and returns the count, handling its own exceptions internally;
  4. closes every resource, and prints a clear, specific message in every catch block.
Must memorise · It writes input.txt and reads output.txt

Part 1 writes input.txt. Part 2 reads output.txt. The program never creates output.txt.

That is not a misprint for you to tidy up. It is the question.

Read part 2 again: "handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist." The examiner has told you, in the question itself, that the file will be missing. The marks are for the catch block running, not for the file being read.

So do not "fix" it by reading input.txt instead. Write exactly what the paper asks, and let the catch block do its job. That is the answer.

MEMORY HOOK: the missing file is the exam. When a question names a file it never created, the catch block is the thing being marked.

Teach · The five classes, and why the list is exactly these five

The restriction looks arbitrary. It is not: the five are exactly what you need and nothing more (Unit 10.3).

ClassDirectionWhat it is for
FileWriteroutWrites characters to a file. On its own it writes one character at a time.
BufferedWriteroutWraps a FileWriter and collects characters, writing them in blocks. Also gives you newLine().
FileReaderinReads characters from a file. On its own it reads one character at a time: it has no readLine().
BufferedReaderinWraps a FileReader and gives you readLine(), which is the whole reason it is on the list.
IOException-The checked exception every one of the above can throw. You must catch it or declare it (Unit 10.1).

The pairing is the point. The question says "read using FileReader" and "one student per line". A FileReader alone cannot give you a line. So you wrap it: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName)). That is why both appear on the list, and it is why the list is not padding.

And read "or its subclasses" carefully. Those three words are permission. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, so you are explicitly allowed to catch it separately, which is exactly how you answer part 2's "including the case where output.txt does not exist" with a message that says what actually happened.

Trap · Catch the child before the parent, or it will not compile

When you catch both, the subclass must come first. Java tries catch blocks top to bottom and takes the first that fits. Put IOException first and it swallows everything, leaving the FileNotFoundException block unreachable. Java does not let that pass:

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.IOException;public class CatchOrder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("any.txt"))) {            System.out.println(in.readLine());        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("the parent is caught first");        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("this line can never run");        }    }}
Compiler outputerror: exception FileNotFoundException has already been caught

This is one of Java's friendlier errors: it refuses to compile code containing a block that could never run. Reverse the two catch blocks and it compiles. Specific first, general last, every time.

Code · question three, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.BufferedWriter;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;public class StudentRecords {    // Part i: create input.txt and write three student records, one per line.    static void writeStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(fileName))) {            out.write("STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92");            out.newLine();            System.out.println("Wrote 3 student records to " + fileName);        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not write to " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part ii: read a file and print every line exactly as it appears.    static void printStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line);                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot read " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while reading " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part iii: count a file's records. Handles its own exceptions; never throws.    static int countRecords(String fileName) {        int lines = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) {                lines++;            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot count " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");            return -1;        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while counting " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());            return -1;        }        return lines;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        writeStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper " +            "asks ---");        printStudents("output.txt");        System.out.println("--- the same method on the file we did write ---");        printStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part iii: counting records ---");        System.out.println("input.txt holds " + countRecords("input.txt")            + " records");        System.out.println("output.txt holds " + countRecords("output.txt")            + " records");    }}
OutputWrote 3 student records to input.txt
--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper asks ---
Cannot read output.txt: the file does not exist.
--- the same method on the file we did write ---
STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51
STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78
STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92
--- part iii: counting records ---
input.txt holds 3 records
Cannot count output.txt: the file does not exist.
output.txt holds -1 records

Line 3 of that output is the 13 marks. The program did exactly what the paper asked, the file was not there, and the catch block said so in words a human can read.

Teach · Four decisions in that program worth defending

1. try-with-resources answers part 4 on its own. Writing try (BufferedWriter out = ...) closes the writer automatically, whether the block ends normally or throws (Unit 10.2). The paper allows a finally block instead, and it is worth knowing why the bracket form is better: a close() inside finally can itself throw, and if it does while an earlier exception is already travelling, the second exception replaces the first and the real cause disappears. If you do use finally, the close must sit inside its own try-catch, and it must test for null, because the resource may have failed to open at all.

2. Wrapping means closing one thing, not two. out.close() on the BufferedWriter closes the FileWriter inside it. Closing the wrapper closes what it wraps, so one bracket handles both.

3. countRecords returns -1, not 0, when it fails. The method must "handle its own exceptions internally", so it cannot throw, so it must return something. Return 0 and the caller cannot tell a missing file from an empty one. -1 is impossible as a line count, so it can only mean failure. A value chosen because it cannot be mistaken for a real answer is called a sentinel, and picking a good one is a real skill.

4. Read the last two lines of the output in the right order. "Cannot count output.txt" prints before "output.txt holds -1 records", even though the second is the println that contains the first as an argument. Java evaluates the arguments before it calls the method: countRecords runs to completion, printing its own message, and only then does the outer println receive -1 and print. Argument first, call second, always.

exam.answer:
Q3 a · define printwriter, files.write(), and try with resources · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. PrintWriter. A character-output class that writes formatted text to a file or stream, giving you the same familiar methods as System.out: print, println and printf. It is a wrapper: you hand it a destination (a file name, or another Writer) and it adds the formatting.
  2. Files.write(). A static method on java.nio.file.Files that writes an entire byte array or collection of lines to a file in a single call, creating the file if needed and closing it for you. It is the one-line alternative to opening a writer, looping, and closing.
  3. try-with-resources. A try with the resource declared in brackets, try (PrintWriter out = ...) { ... }, which automatically closes that resource when the block ends, whether it ends normally or by an exception. It removes the need for a finally block whose only job is closing. Unit 10.2.

Where the marks are: for each, say what it is and what it saves you. "PrintWriter writes formatted text" earns the mark; "PrintWriter is for files" does not distinguish it from FileWriter.

exam.answer:
Q3 b · debug filetest · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: class, interface, enum, or record expected

The errors, listed.

  1. Line 1 is missing import. java.io.FileWriter; on its own is not a statement, it is nothing at all, which is why javac's first complaint is that it expected a class. Fix: import java.io.FileWriter;
  2. FileWriter("note.txt") is missing new. Creating an object requires new: without it Java looks for a method called FileWriter and finds none. Fix: new FileWriter("note.txt").
  3. writer.close is missing its brackets and semicolon. A method call needs (). Fix: writer.close(); Naming a method without calling it is not a statement, so it cannot stand on a line by itself.
  4. The IOException is never handled. This is the error the others hide, and it is the one worth the mark. new FileWriter(...), write(...) and close() all throw IOException, which is checked (Unit 10.1), so the code will not compile until you either catch it or declare throws IOException on main. Fix all three syntax errors and it still does not compile.

Error 4 is the one that separates answers. Anyone can see a missing bracket; the examiner wants to know whether you understand that a checked exception is a compile-time obligation.

Code · q3 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;public class FileTest {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (FileWriter writer = new FileWriter("note.txt")) {            writer.write("Hello from Java!");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not write note.txt: " + e.getMessage());        }        System.out.println("note.txt written");    }}
Outputnote.txt written

try-with-resources answers error 3 and error 4 together: it closes the writer for you, so close() cannot be forgotten, and the catch discharges the checked exception. That is Q3 A part 3 being examined in part B.

exam.answer:
Q3 c · what is the output of the data.txt file? · 4 MARKS

Note the question: not what the program prints on screen (it prints nothing), but what ends up in the file.

The answer:

data.txtAge: 25
Score: 89.46

Two lines. And three details carry the four marks.

Must memorise · print, println, printf: the three differences

print("Age: ")   writes the text, no line break. So the 25 lands on the same line.

println(25)   writes it and a line break. That break is what ends line 1.

printf("Score: %.2f", 89.456)   formats, and adds no line break unless you write %n.

1. %.2f rounds, it does not truncate. 89.456 to two places is 89.46, not 89.45. Unit 3.11.

2. The file has no trailing newline. printf did not add one, so the file ends immediately after the 6 of 89.46. The file is 21 bytes and its last character is not a line break.

3. Nothing appears on screen. Every call is on pw, not on System.out. A common wrong answer is to write the two lines as program output.

MEMORY HOOK: only println breaks the line. print and printf leave the cursor exactly where it stopped.

Code · the paper's code, plus a dump of the file it wrote · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.*;public class PrintWriterExample {    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter("data.txt");        pw.print("Age: ");        pw.println(25);        pw.printf("Score: %.2f", 89.456);        pw.close();        // show exactly what landed in the file, bytes and all        BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();        int c;        while ((c = in.read()) != -1) sb.append((char) c);        in.close();        System.out.println("--- data.txt verbatim ---");        System.out.print(sb);        System.out.println("\n--- as escaped bytes ---");        System.out.println(sb.toString().replace("\r", "\r").replace("\n", "\n"));        System.out.println("length = " + sb.length());    }}
Output--- data.txt verbatim ---
Age: 25
Score: 89.46
--- as escaped bytes ---
Age: 25
Score: 89.46
length = 21

The paper's four lines are exactly as printed; everything after pw.close() is ours, reading the file back so that this book can show you what landed in it. Length 21 is the proof of the trailing-newline point: "Age: 25" is 7 characters, "Score: 89.46" is 12, which is 19, and the two remaining bytes are the single line break in the middle. There is nothing on the end.

Those two bytes are worth a word. println uses the platform's line separator, which on Windows is carriage-return plus line-feed (two characters) and on Linux is line-feed alone (one). Same program, 21 bytes here and 20 there. The two printed lines are the answer either way; if you are asked for a byte count, say which platform.

exam.answer:
Q3 d · write students.txt as a formatted, appended table · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · PrintWriter cannot append. The FileWriter under it can

new PrintWriter("students.txt")   truncates the file to empty. Every time. There is no append constructor.

new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("students.txt", true))   appends.

The true is the append flag, and it belongs to FileWriter, not to PrintWriter. So the answer to "append with PrintWriter" is to wrap one around a FileWriter opened in append mode, exactly as Unit 10.3 wraps a BufferedReader around a FileReader to get readLine(). Each wrapper adds what the other lacks.

And it satisfies part i for free. FileWriter creates the file if it does not exist, in either mode. So "create students.txt if it does not exist" needs no if, no File.exists(), no check at all: opening it in append mode does both jobs.

MEMORY HOOK: the flag is on the writer that touches the disk. PrintWriter only formats; FileWriter opens the file, so the mode is its business.

Code · q3 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.PrintWriter;public class StudentTable {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String[] names = {"John", "Lilian", "Ken"};        int[] ages = {20, 21, 19};        double[] gpas = {3.75, 3.95, 3.65};        // iv. APPEND, not overwrite. new PrintWriter("students.txt") would truncate        // the file each run; the append flag is on the FileWriter beneath.        // i. A dot marks each trailing space from printf's padding.        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("students.txt"))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line.replace(' ', '.'));                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not read students.txt back: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}
students.txt, read back, every space shown as a dotName.....Age...GPA...
John.....20....3.75..
Lilian...21....3.95..
Ken......19....3.65..

The dots are the marks. %-8s means: a String, left aligned, padded to 8 columns, and you can count the padding: "Name" plus four dots, "Lilian" plus two. The minus sign is what makes it left aligned; drop it and every column is pushed right and the table goes ragged. %-6.2f is the same idea for a double, fixed at 2 decimal places, which is why 3.75 prints as 3.75 and not 3.8. Unit 3.11.

Those trailing dots are real spaces, sitting at the end of every line. printf pads the last column just as faithfully as the others, because it cannot know it is last. Harmless in a text file, and worth knowing before you go looking for why two files that "look identical" are not.

Code · proof that the append flag is doing the work · RUN TWICE, IN ONE PROGRAM

The claim above is that the true is what makes it append and that without it the file is wiped. Here that claim is tested: the same write is done twice each way, and the lines are counted.

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.PrintWriter;public class AppendProof {    static void writeOnce(String file, boolean append) throws IOException {        try (PrintWriter out = append                ? new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(file, true))   // appends                : new PrintWriter(file)) {                      // TRUNCATES            out.printf("%-8s %-5d %-6.2f%n", "John", 20, 3.75);        }    }    static int lines(String file) throws IOException {        int n = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) n++;        }        return n;    }    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        writeOnce("appended.txt", true);        writeOnce("appended.txt", true);        System.out.println("new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(f, true)) twice -> "            + lines("appended.txt") + " lines");        writeOnce("truncated.txt", false);        writeOnce("truncated.txt", false);        System.out.println("new PrintWriter(f)                     twice -> "            + lines("truncated.txt") + " lines");    }}
Outputnew PrintWriter(new FileWriter(f, true)) twice -> 2 lines
new PrintWriter(f)                     twice -> 1 lines

Two lines against one. The appending version kept both records; the plain PrintWriter threw the first away and left only the second. If you write new PrintWriter("students.txt") in the exam, your program passes every other part of this question and still fails part iv, and nothing in its output tells you.
